How much does Mercari take per sale?

Mercari changed its US seller fee structure for listings created or updated on or after January 6, 2025. The current schedule is a single 10% selling fee, charged on the item price plus any shipping the buyer paid, with no separate payment processing fee. A listing made before that date keeps the old schedule — 10% on the item price only, plus a payment processing fee of 2.9% of the combined total plus a flat $0.50 — until you edit it.

The current-schedule formula

fee = 10% × (item price + buyer-paid shipping)

payout = item price + buyer-paid shipping − fee − your own shipping-label cost

Mercari also charges the buyer a separate 3.6% Buyer Protection Fee, on top of what they pay — it never reduces the seller's payout, and is not part of this formula at all.

Worked example 1: $50 item, no buyer-paid shipping

LineAmount
Item price$50.00
Selling fee (10% of $50.00)$5.00
Payout$45.00

Worked example 2: the fee reaches shipping too

LineAmount
Item price$20.00
Buyer-paid shipping$6.00
Combined$26.00
Selling fee (10% of $26.00)$2.60
Payout$23.40

Not $2.00 (10% of the $20 item price alone) — the fee is on the combined $26.00. This is the detail sellers most often get wrong on a listing where the buyer pays shipping separately.

The legacy schedule: 10% + 2.9% + $0.50

A listing created before January 6, 2025 that has not since been edited still runs the old schedule: 10% of the item price only, plus a payment processing fee of 2.9% of the combined item-plus-shipping total, plus a flat $0.50 per order. On the same $50 item with no shipping, that is $5.00 selling fee + ($50 × 2.9% + $0.50) = $1.95 processing fee = $6.95 total, for a $43.05 payout — $1.95 less than the current schedule pays on the same sale, because the current schedule dropped the processing fee entirely.

The comparison flips when most of the price is shipping: the legacy schedule only taxes shipping at 2.9%, while the current schedule taxes it at the full 10%, so a listing with a large buyer-paid shipping charge can net more under the old schedule. Use the calculator's "Compare both schedules" button to check a specific sale rather than assuming either direction.

Do this with your own listings

The Mercari fee calculator runs this same arithmetic on your own item price, shipping, and costs, solves for the price you need to hit a target profit, and compares both schedules side by side. Nothing you type leaves your browser.

Common questions

How much does Mercari take on a $50 sale?

Under the current schedule (listings created or updated on or after January 6, 2025): 10% of $50, which is $5.00, leaving a $45.00 payout, assuming no buyer-paid shipping.

How much does Mercari take when the buyer pays for shipping?

The 10% fee applies to the item price plus the buyer-paid shipping combined. A $20 item with $6 buyer-paid shipping pays 10% of $26, which is $2.60 — not 10% of the $20 item price alone.

What was Mercari's fee before January 6, 2025?

A 10% selling fee on the item price only, plus a separate payment processing fee of 2.9% of the item price plus buyer-paid shipping, plus a flat $0.50 per order. A listing made before that date keeps this schedule until it is edited.

No warranty. This page is free arithmetic, not legal, tax, financial, or selling advice. Rates change and are set by Mercari, not by this site. Verify every figure against your own Mercari payout statement before you price a listing. Not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Mercari; Mercari is a trademark of its owner, named here only to describe the published fee schedule.

vs-doing-the-fee-math-yourself.html.text:
← Mercari Fee Calculator

This calculator vs. doing Mercari fee math yourself

10% of the item price is the easy part, and most sellers can do that in their head. What mental math cannot see is which of Mercari's two fee schedules a listing actually runs, or that the current schedule's 10% reaches buyer-paid shipping too — so the same "just take 10%" instinct produces a confidently wrong number the moment shipping or an older listing is involved.

What each approach actually does

Doing it yourself gets the right answer for the one case where the math really is just 10% of the item price: a current-schedule sale (listing created or updated on or after January 6, 2025) with no buyer-paid shipping. Add buyer-paid shipping, or an older listing that might still be on the legacy schedule, and mental math has to guess at two things it cannot see from the headline rate alone — what the fee base includes, and which schedule applies at all.

This calculator already applies the right formula for whichever schedule you tell it: the current schedule's 10% on item price plus buyer-paid shipping with no separate processing fee, or the legacy schedule's 10% on item price only plus a 2.9% + $0.50 processing fee — and it can compare both side by side when you are not sure which one an old, unedited listing is still running.

QuestionWhere to answer it
Current-schedule item, no buyer-paid shipping.Either way — 10% of the item price, correctly, in your head.
Buyer pays for shipping separately.This calculator — the 10% base is item price plus shipping, easy to under-count by hand.
An old listing I haven't edited since before January 6, 2025.This calculator's schedule comparison — the legacy processing fee is easy to forget entirely.
Does the 3.6% Buyer Protection Fee come out of my payout?Neither approach subtracts it — it's the buyer's cost, not the seller's, either way.
Is my data uploaded anywhere?No. Everything runs in your browser; your sale figures stay on this device.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and nothing you type is uploaded anywhere.

Common questions

Isn't Mercari's fee just 10% -- why would I get the math wrong doing it myself?

Because 10% of what is the part that trips people up, not the rate itself. Under the current schedule (listings created or updated on or after January 6, 2025), the 10% applies to the item price plus any shipping the buyer paid -- so a $20 item with $6 buyer-paid shipping pays 10% of $26 ($2.60), not 10% of the $20 item price alone ($2.00). Doing the multiplication in your head against the wrong base gives you a confidently wrong number every time, not an occasional slip.

When is doing it yourself actually fine?

A current-schedule sale with no buyer-paid shipping: take 10% of the item price and you have the fee, correctly, in your head. The moment shipping enters the picture, or the listing is old enough that you are not sure which schedule it runs, mental math starts guessing at inputs it cannot see -- which schedule, and what the fee base actually includes -- rather than just doing arithmetic wrong.

What does manual math most often get wrong here?

Three things, in rough order of how often they bite: forgetting the current schedule's 10% reaches buyer-paid shipping, not just the item price; forgetting that a legacy (pre-January-2025, unedited) listing adds a separate 2.9% + $0.50 processing fee on top of its 10% selling fee, so the two schedules are not both simply '10%'; and folding the buyer's 3.6% Buyer Protection Fee into the seller-side deduction, when it is charged to the buyer on top of what they pay and never reduces the seller's payout at all.

Does this replace checking my actual payout statement?

No, and it is not built to. Both a mental calculation and this calculator are estimates from the fee schedule as published; Mercari can change that schedule, and your own payout statement is the only record of what a specific sale actually settled at. Verify against that statement before you rely on either estimate for pricing decisions.

vs-poshmark.html.text:
← Mercari Fee Calculator

Mercari vs. Poshmark: the same sale, both fee schedules

Mercari's 10% sounds cheaper than Poshmark's 20%. Whether it actually is depends on something neither headline rate mentions: who pays for the shipping label. This worked example prices one $50 item both ways.

The item

A $50 item that cost $20 and needs $1 of packaging either way. On Mercari, the seller lists with "free shipping" and buys their own $8 label — a common choice, and the current 10% fee (listings created or updated on or after January 6, 2025) applies to the item price alone since the buyer pays no shipping. On Poshmark, the sale clears the $15 commission threshold, so Poshmark keeps 20% of the sale price; the buyer pays Poshmark's own flat shipping fee separately at checkout, which funds a prepaid label and never touches what the seller receives.

On a $50 saleMercariPoshmark
Fee / commission$5.00 (10% of $50)$10.00 (20% of $50)
Shipping label$8.00 (seller-bought)$0.00 (buyer pays it separately)
Item cost$20.00$20.00
Packaging$1.00$1.00
Total fees + shipping$13.00$10.00
Net payout$37.00$40.00
Net profit$16.00$19.00
Margin32.0%38.0%

On this free-shipping listing, Poshmark nets $3.00 more — its higher commission is still less than Mercari's fee plus the label the seller bought out of pocket.

The real lever: who pays for shipping

Change one thing about the Mercari listing — charge the buyer $8 for shipping instead of folding it into the price — and the result flips. Mercari's 10% now reaches that $8 too ($5.80 fee on $58 combined), but the seller no longer pays for the label out of their own payout:

Same $50 item, buyer pays Mercari shippingMercariPoshmark
Fee (10% of $58 combined)$5.80$10.00 (20% of $50)
Shipping label$0.00 (covered by buyer's $8 payment)$0.00
Item cost + packaging$21.00$21.00
Net profit$23.20$19.00

Mercari now nets $4.20 more. Nothing about either fee schedule changed between the two tables — only who ends up paying for the label. Poshmark's per-sale cost to the seller is always just its commission, because shipping is never the seller's to pay on that platform. Mercari's per-sale cost is its 10% fee plus whatever shipping cost the seller does not pass to the buyer, so the same item can net more on either platform depending on that one listing choice.

What this comparison cannot tell you

  • Your item's actual shipping cost isn't $8. A heavier or bulkier item costs more to ship on Mercari and makes Poshmark's no-seller-shipping structure look better; a light, cheap-to-ship item narrows or closes the gap. Replace $8 with your own label cost.
  • Poshmark's buyer-paid shipping fee isn't modeled here. It doesn't touch seller payout either way, so it does not belong in this comparison — but it does affect what a buyer is willing to pay, which this page cannot see.
  • An older Mercari listing may be on the legacy schedule (10% + 2.9% + $0.50), not the current 10%-only schedule this page uses. See the Mercari calculator's own schedule comparison for that case.
  • Neither platform's audience, sell-through speed, or negotiation norms are compared here. This page prices one hypothetical sale on each platform's published fee schedule — it says nothing about which one sells a given item faster or for a higher accepted price.

Common questions

Is Mercari or Poshmark cheaper?

It depends on who pays for shipping, not just the headline rate. On the $50 worked example here, a free-shipping Mercari listing where the seller buys an $8 label nets $16 profit; the same item on Poshmark, where the buyer's flat shipping fee never touches seller payout, nets $19. But if the Mercari seller instead charges the buyer for that same $8 of shipping, Mercari's 10% fee wins instead, netting about $23.20. Mercari's lower headline rate only wins once shipping cost stops coming out of the seller's own pocket.

Why does the cheaper platform depend on who pays for shipping?

Mercari's 10% fee is charged on the item price plus any shipping the buyer pays — so a seller who charges the buyer for shipping pays a bit more fee on that shipping, but keeps the label cost out of their own pocket entirely. A seller who offers "free shipping" instead absorbs the label cost directly, which is not a Mercari fee but comes out of the same payout. Poshmark's 20%-or-$2.95 commission is the only deduction from a Poshmark seller's payout: shipping is a flat fee the buyer pays separately at checkout, funding a prepaid label that never reduces what the seller receives, regardless of the item's actual weight or shipping cost. 20% sounds larger than 10%, but it is also the seller's only per-sale cost on Poshmark, where Mercari's 10% is often only part of one.

Does this account for Mercari's legacy fee schedule?

No — this page only models Mercari's current schedule (listings created or updated on or after January 6, 2025): 10% on item price plus buyer-paid shipping, no separate processing fee. An older, unedited Mercari listing may still run the legacy 10% + 2.9% + $0.50 schedule, which changes the Mercari side of this comparison. Use the Mercari calculator's own schedule comparison to check which one a specific listing is on before comparing it to Poshmark.

Is this page affiliated with Poshmark?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Poshmark. Poshmark is a trademark of its owner, named here only to describe its published seller fee schedule, using a worked example rather than a claim about either platform's current rates for your specific item.

Open the Mercari fee calculator for your own item, or see the Poshmark fee calculator for the $2.95-under-$15/20%-at-$15+ cliff on its own.
